working_title: Electric or Push Trolley: How to Actually Choose the Right One for UK Courses
angle: Most 'electric vs push' articles treat this as a pure features comparison, but the real decision hinges on three practical UK-specific factors: how hilly your regular courses are, how much boot space you have, and how often you play. The post cuts through the noise by framing the choice around those factors rather than a generic spec sheet.
research_notes:
- Electric trolleys are battery-powered and drive themselves; push (three-wheel) trolleys require the golfer to push manually — the core difference is effort and cost (sources: golfgeardirect, trolleyguru)
- Electric trolleys are heavier and bulkier than push trolleys due to integrated motor, battery, and gearbox; push trolleys are lighter and fold smaller, making them easier to store and transport (sources: golfgeardirect, todays-golfer, golf monthly)
- Push trolleys generally offer more storage as standard than most electric models (sources: todays-golfer, today's golfer via golf monthly)
- Battery sizing matters for electric buyers: an 18-hole lithium battery covers a standard round; 27- and 36-hole batteries suit hilly courses or back-to-back rounds (source: trolleyguru)
- On hilly UK courses, downhill braking systems on electric trolleys (e.g. Motocaddy M1 DHC) prevent the trolley running away on descents — a real practical concern on many UK heathland and links layouts (source: golf-gear.co.uk)
- Electric trolleys typically start around £499 (e.g. Motocaddy SE) and can reach £1,600–£1,900 for follow/remote models such as the Stewart Golf Q Follow (sources: thegolfshoponline, golfgeardirect360)
- Push trolleys sit at a significantly lower price point; e.g. PowaKaddy Micra cited at £189, Clicgear 4.0 at £219 (source: thegolfshoponline push trolley guide)
- The Stewart Golf Q Follow uses Bluetooth to follow the golfer hands-free — the premium end of the market (source: golf-gear.co.uk)
- Key brands in UK electric market: Motocaddy, PowaKaddy, Stewart Golf, MGI, Hill Billy (source: trolleyguru)
- Key brands in push market: PowaKaddy (Micra), Motocaddy (Cube, P1), Clicgear (4.0), Big Max, Bag Boy (sources: moresports, launchpointgolf)
- For a regular weekend walker on flat-to-moderate UK courses, a quality push trolley delivers most practical benefit at a fraction of the cost and weight of an electric (source: launchpointgolf)
- Boot space is a genuine practical concern for UK golfers: electric trolleys fold compactly but remain heavier to lift; push trolleys dismantle smaller and suit smaller car boots (sources: golf monthly, todays-golfer)
- Features worth paying for on electric: GPS integration, downhill braking, remote/follow capability, compact fold — reliability and fold size matter more to most owners than headline GPS or remote features (source: golfgeardirect360)
- Features worth paying for on push: solid braking on slopes, lightweight frame, quick-fold mechanism, storage compartments
- Frequency of play is a key financial consideration: electric models make most sense for golfers playing regularly enough to justify the outlay (source: golf monthly)
